title: What are you doing today?
title_target: Что ты делаешь? — Shto ty delayesh?
goal: Talk about your daily activities, master the second verb group, and learn a rule that sounds wrong but is compulsory: in Russian, negation is used twice.
bekal: conjugate Group II verbs for all six persons
say how often you do something
use double negatives with никогда, ничего, никто
tell говорить, сказать and разговаривать apart
hold a casual conversation with ты

dialogs.title: Диалог — An afternoon in the canteen
dialogs.intro: Ani and Марко are now close enough to use ты. Notice the word никогда in line six: there are two negatives in one sentence, and that is exactly right.

lines.speaker: Марко:
lines.id: What do you usually do in the evenings?

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Watch series and learn vocabulary. And you?
lines.literal: watch — series — and — learn — words. and — you?

lines.speaker: Марко:
lines.id: I love cooking. I often make pasta.
lines.literal: I — love — to-cook. often — cook — pasta.

lines.speaker: Марко:
lines.id: And do you cook Indonesian food?

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: I never cook. I can't cook at all.
lines.literal: I — never — not — cook. at-all — not — know-how.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: I eat in the canteen. Or I buy something.
lines.literal: eat — in — canteen. or — buy — anything.

lines.speaker: Марко:
lines.id: Terrible! Come on Saturday, I'll teach you.
lines.literal: horror! come — on — Saturday, I — will-teach — you.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Really? Thanks! I can't do anything, but I learn fast.
lines.literal: really? thank-you! I — nothing — not — know-how, but — I — quickly — learn.

lines.speaker: Марко:
lines.literal: great. then — on — Saturday, at — six.

notes: **Negation is used TWICE, and it's compulsory.** ⚠️ *Я **никогда не** готовлю* is literally "I never don't cook" — but it means "I never cook". Same with *Я **ничего не** знаю* (I don't know anything) and *Здесь **никого нет*** (there's nobody here). To English speakers, taught that "double negatives" are bad grammar, this feels like a logic error. Just accept it as a rule: **if there's a word starting with ни-, the verb MUST have не in front.** Dropping the не is a mistake, not a simplification.

**Group II has the endings -ю / -ишь.** The difference from Group I is the vowel in the ending: Group I uses **е** (работа**е**шь), Group II uses **и** (говор**и**шь). There's no sure way to tell a verb's group from its dictionary form; most verbs ending in **-ить** are Group II, and that's a pretty good guess.

**Some Group II verbs slip in an -л- in the я form.** любить → лю**бл**ю, готовить → гото**вл**ю, купить → ку**пл**ю. The rule: if the root ends in б, в, м, п or ф, an **л** appears — but **only in the я form**. The other forms are normal: ты любишь, он любит.

**Люблю means both "like" and "love", and it's not as heavy as it sounds.** *Я люблю кофе* isn't dramatic at all — it's as ordinary as "I love coffee" in English. The word only gets heavy when the object is a person: *Я люблю тебя*. For lighter liking there's нравиться, which comes in Unit 15.

**Же is a little word that adds flavor, not meaning.** *Ты **же** итальянец!* ≈ "you're Italian, after all!". It stresses something that should already be obvious. English has no single equivalent; "after all", "of course" or a stressed "you ARE" come closest.

**Умею means "can" because you have the skill, not "can" because you're allowed.** *Я не умею готовить* — I can't cook (I don't have the skill). For "may, it's allowed" there's можно, for "be physically able" there's могу. ⚠️ English uses one word "can" for all three; Russian keeps them strictly apart.
**Что-нибудь means "anything, something".** Its partners: кто-нибудь (anyone), где-нибудь (anywhere), когда-нибудь (ever, sometime). The ending -нибудь always means "any, unspecified".

grammars.title: Group II verbs — endings -ю / -ишь
body: Drop **-ить** from the dictionary form, then add the ending. Compare the first column with the Group I table in Unit 5: only the vowel is different.
after: Other verbs that follow this pattern: **учить** (to learn by heart), **готовить** (to cook), **видеть** (to see), **слышать** (to hear), **помнить** (to remember), **стоить** (to cost), **звонить** (to call).

⚠️ Watch the stress in смотреть: in the **я** form it's on the ending (*smat-RYU*), in the other forms it moves to the root (*SMOT-rish*). Stress shifts like this are common and can't be guessed — which is why every form in this course carries its own pronunciation.

grammars.title: How often
body: Frequency adverbs never change form. They most often go before the verb.
after: *Я **всегда** пью кофе утром.* — I always drink coffee in the morning.
*Я **никогда не** пью кофе вечером.* — I never drink coffee in the evening. Note that compulsory **не**.

blocks.text: English uses "speak", "say" and "talk" fairly loosely. Russian keeps three meanings apart, and picking the wrong one is instantly noticeable.

rows: Скажите, пожалуйста… — Could you tell me…

blocks.title: The most useful opening line in Russia
items: **Скажите, пожалуйста…** (*ska-ZHY-tye pa-ZHA-loos-ta*) — "Could you tell me…". This is the standard way to start a question to a stranger in the street, at a station, in a shop. Far more polite than just firing off the question.
**Можно вопрос?** (*MOZH-na va-PROS*) — "May I ask a question?". Used in class and in meetings.
⚠️ Don't start with **Эй!** or jump straight into your question. Russians are famous for a blank face toward strangers in the street, but Скажите, пожалуйста almost always opens the door.
